claims.text: Controlled coherent high-thermal-conductivity nanoprecipitates will enhance the heat-transfer capability of an HEA intermediate layer.
The nanoprecipitate intervention will maintain structural integrity under plasma-facing reactor conditions.
A standard HEA intermediate layer has a primarily single-phase microstructure.
Thermal-mechanical processing can induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a refractory HEA.
The induced nanoprecipitates can be distributed uniformly within the HEA matrix.
Tungsten-rich nanoprecipitates would be high-thermal-conductivity particles.
The proposed enhancement will hold at temperatures up to approximately 800 degrees Celsius.
The proposed enhancement will hold under cyclic mechanical loading representative of plasma-reactor service.
Coherent matrix-precipitate interfaces provide enhanced pathways for thermal transport.
Coherent nanoprecipitates impede dislocation motion.
Coherent nanoprecipitates control grain growth.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations that could cause premature cracking.
Nanoprecipitates provide parallel channels for phonon and electron transport.
Parallel phonon and electron transport through the nanoprecipitates increases thermal conductivity.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can reinforce a refractory HEA while retaining useful ductility and high-temperature strength.
The modified HEA will have higher thermal conductivity than the unmodified HEA.
The modified HEA will maintain mechanical strength and structural stability comparable to current intermediate materials.
Current intermediate-layer HEAs without induced nanoprecipitates have lower heat-transfer efficiency and are designed primarily for mechanical strength.
Excessive nanoprecipitate density or overly large precipitates may cause brittleness.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant thermal-conductivity improvement while limiting the strength reduction to less than 10%, or occurrence of premature failure, would falsify the hypothesis.
